title: Archimedes Yelled Eureka Naked? Told Nearly 200 Yrs Later｜Curio Archive
description:
Did Archimedes really run naked into the street shouting Eureka? The earliest record of that scene was written nearly 200 years after him.
For anyone who grew up with this story and wants to know where history's famous scenes really come from.

This episode sticks to what the records say, going through them one by one in order: the Roman architect Vitruvius's Ten Books on Architecture, Archimedes' own surviving On Floating Bodies, Plutarch more than a century later, a Latin poem by an unknown author from the late Roman Empire, and The Little Balance, a short essay Galileo wrote for friends in 1586, in his early twenties. Each tells the bath a little differently: some have a bathtub and some don't, some say he ran and others that he walked, and someone even calls the way the crown was measured too crude.

Finally, mathematician Chris Rorres does the math on that water: how far apart are measuring the water and weighing on a balance under water? His numbers are for a hypothetical wreath. As for the naked run home, only one ancient record tells it. No evidence says it happened, and none says it didn't, so this case is still open. Sources are listed below.

Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated.

Data as of 2026-10-20

chapters.plutarch: Over a century on, he walked

ek001.text: You know this one: Archimedes got into a bath, saw it overflow, and cracked a hard problem.

ek002.text: Overjoyed, he ran naked into the street shouting Eureka, meaning: I found it.

ek003.text: You've likely heard it since childhood. Yet the earliest written account is nearly 200 years later.

ek004.text: Stranger: a version over 100 years later is missing something.

ek005.text: Over 1,000 years on, a man in his early twenties read of the method and slammed it.

ek006.text: Today: did Archimedes really run naked down the street shouting Eureka?

ek007.text: We'll open every record of this bath in date order: five ancient texts, one calculation.

ek008.text: The earliest known account is by a Roman architect, Vitruvius.

ek009.text: A military engineer, he oversaw Augustus's catapults.

ek010.text: He wrote De architectura for Augustus, in the late first century BC.

ek011.text: From Archimedes' death to then: those nearly 200 years.

ek012.text: So where did he hear this story?

ek013.text: The book doesn't say a word. Every time, I want to ask him.

ek014.text: It opens Book 9. Hiero, king of Syracuse, ruled the city over half a century.

ek015.text: As new king, he vowed a temple a gold crown.

ek016.text: Called a crown, it was really a wreath of gold leaves; forget the jeweled one.

ek017.text: Remember this wreath: several records come back to it.

ek018.text: The king weighed out gold to a craftsman to make a wreath of that weight;

ek019.text: On delivery day, the wreath was weighed: exactly the right weight.

ek021.text: An informer claimed he'd swapped some gold for equal-weight silver.

ek022.text: But it was for the gods: no melting, no scraping.

ek023.text: Furious but stumped, the king asked Archimedes to think. The result?

ek024.text: Just then, he happened into a public bath, the problem on his mind.

ek025.text: As he sat, the deeper he sank, the more water spilled.

ek027.text: The overflow showed him the way:

ek028.text: A thing in water displaces its own volume; equal weights of gold and silver differ in size.

ek029.text: He leapt from the bath, overjoyed,

ek030.text: and headed home naked, shouting as he ran:

ek031.text: Eureka, Eureka! Meaning: I found it.

ek032.text: Wait. By this text, did he run naked through the streets?

ek033.text: Look closely: it says "homeward," not the street;

ek034.text: and he ran home from a public bath, not out of his tub.

ek035.text: "Forgot his clothes," "ran all over town": later layers, one by one.

ek036.text: That's how your childhood street-run version grew.

ek038.text: The Latin sometimes means just in a tunic;

ek039.text: But he'd just leapt from the bath; read literally, it means naked.

ek042.text: Vitruvius continues, adding a hedge first: reportedly.

ek043.text: He reportedly made gold and silver lumps as heavy as the wreath, and put each in a full vessel,

ek044.text: then used a Roman measure, cup by cup, to see how much water refilled it.

ek045.text: The wreath displaced more than the equal gold lump; that's how the silver was exposed.

ek046.text: Makes sense, right? Hold on, someone later isn't buying it.

ek049.text: But why tell this in a book on building?

ek050.text: Because Book 9 opens, a bit comically, with a defense of writers:

ek051.text: Writers deserve the honors athletes get, and more.

ek052.text: Archimedes is one of his examples; the one before is Pythagoras.

ek053.text: And Archimedes himself? Did he ever write about this wreath?

ek054.text: At least in his surviving works, not one word on a crown, or a bath.

ek055.text: In 1897, British scholar Heath edited his works in English

ek057.text: Cover to cover, "crown" appears only in the editor's intro and notes.

ek058.text: Some of his books were lost; some survived by sheer luck. How lucky?

ek059.text: On Floating Bodies' Greek text was later found in a scraped, reused parchment.

ek060.text: And On Floating Bodies is exactly about things in water.

ek061.text: It says a thing heavier than water weighs less in water,

ek062.text: losing the weight of water it pushes aside.

ek063.text: That's textbook buoyancy. But here's the thing: he's talking about weighing in water.

ek064.text: The overflowing bath compared volume, not this book's idea.

ek066.text: How did other ancients tell this bath?

ek067.text: That version 100-plus years later is by Greek writer Plutarch.

ek068.text: He first adds "it is said": by his time, this was already a story going around.

ek069.text: It's said spilled bathwater showed him a crown test;

ek070.text: as if possessed, he leapt out shouting "I found it," and went off shouting.

ek071.text: He tells it to mock gluttons: no gourmet has ever finished a meal shouting "I've eaten it!"

ek072.text: Ever dash out yelling after a feast?

ek074.text: So what's the missing thing? Nakedness: Plutarch says not a word about clothes;

ek075.text: nor that he went home; his word is "went," not "ran."

ek076.text: Plutarch elsewhere relays a rumor: often dragged to be bathed, oiled,

ek077.text: tracing geometry on his oiled skin.

ek078.text: No wonder the story fits him so well; that's my guess.

ek079.text: A bath, but no nakedness. Is there a version with no bath?

ek080.text: Yes. A late Roman Latin poem by an unknown author clearly tells the same story:

ek081.text: a king of Sicily, a gold crown for the gods, a craftsman mixing in silver;

ek082.text: but no bath, and nobody shouts "I found it";

ek083.text: Not even Archimedes' name, just "the master of Syracuse."

ek084.text: It uses a balance: equal weights of gold and silver on each side, level,

ek085.text: then both go into water; the gold side sinks at once.

ek086.text: Same crown: one way measures water, one weighs. Which actually works?

ek087.text: The water method was mocked back in 1586;

ek088.text: the critic was that young man: Italy's Galileo.

ek089.text: A short essay for friends, unpublished in his life, later named La bilancetta.

ek090.text: He opens: as some write, put the crown in water and judge gold from silver by the rise;

ek091.text: this idea, frankly, is crude and far from exact.

ek092.text: He says "some have written," naming no one. So where did the water part come from?

ek093.text: His guess: word spread of Archimedes exposing the theft with water; a writer then wrote it down,

ek094.text: and, to pad out the little he'd heard, added the water method.

ek095.text: To us, it's the best line in the whole file: the water part is suspected to be the writer's own addition.

ek096.text: Still, that's his guess, not proof; and he doubted only the method, not the bath.

ek097.text: Beyond friends, did anyone print this doubt?

ek098.text: Yes. In 1589, another Italian wrote in a printed book that it was hard to use;

ek100.text: What did Galileo think Archimedes used?

ek101.text: A balance. Like that poem, weighing it in water.

ek102.text: Remember On Floating Bodies? Galileo said this was Archimedes' way,

ek103.text: because it rests on what that book proved.

ek104.text: You may wonder: if crude, how far off could it be?

ek105.text: Mathematician Chris Rorres did the math. His assumption: a 1-kilogram wreath.

ek106.text: The largest wreath of that era actually unearthed weighs over 700 grams; rounding to 1 kilogram seems fair to me.

ek107.text: 30% of the gold now silver; vessel mouth 20 cm.

ek108.text: Wreath versus equal-weight gold: how much does the water level differ?

ek110.text: The water gap wasn't small: about three dice;

ek111.text: yet drop three dice in a basin, and the surface barely moves.

ek112.text: What about weighing it in water?

ek114.text: he says scales of Archimedes' day could easily detect that.

ek115.text: In 2006, he told Scientific American: the water method works in theory;

ek116.text: but in practice, reality gets in the way. What exactly?

ek117.text: He named three spoilers: surface tension, water clinging as it's lifted out, and air bubbles in the wreath.

ek118.text: Method likely fails. And the bath, the "I found it"?

ek119.text: Rorres says the story may hold some truth: Archimedes did measure volumes;

ek120.text: but his "I found it" moment may have been finding buoyancy,

ek121.text: not from a bath and a naked street run.

ek122.text: Back to the question: did he really run naked in the street shouting Eureka?

ek123.text: Look back: the earliest record says homeward, not the street;

ek124.text: Plutarch, 100-plus years on, never even mentions clothes;

ek125.text: over 1,000 years on, even the water method was called crude. So did it happen?

ek126.text: The naked run home has only one record: that Roman architect's.

ek127.text: Whether it happened, no evidence can say. This case is still open.

ek128.text: We can check what each record says and doesn't; we can't answer what really happened that day.

ek129.text: Each retelling may add a layer or lose a piece. What did it first look like?

ek131.text: In the version you grew up with, was he dressed as he ran? Comment below.

ek132.text: We only cover what's on record; subscribe to open the files with us.
